blocks.text: That John the Baptist had real locusts for food.

It has been shown so far that there is scarcely any animal more destructive to the human race than locusts. [col. 488] Yet these too have their use, which others explain at length. It will be enough for us to show that locusts served as food for not a few peoples long ago, and still serve so today, with regard to the much-discussed (πολυθρύλλητα [polythryllēta]) words about John the Baptist in Matth. III, 4: Ἡ δὲ τροφὴ αὐτοῦ ἦν ἀκρίδες, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον [Hē de trophē autou ēn akrides, kai meli agrion]. And Marc. I, 6.: Ἐσθίων ἀκρίδας, καὶ μέλι ἄγριον [Esthiōn akridas, kai meli agrion]. Although these words teach clearly and openly that locusts and wild honey were his food, nevertheless, as though it were intolerable to believe that the holy man sustained his life on locusts, many ancients and moderns have twisted themselves into every shape in order to bend these words to another sense. The Ebionites lead the column; in their Gospel the following was read about John: Τὸ βρῶμα αὐτοῦ μέλι ἄγριον, οὗ ἡ γεῦσις ἦν τοῦ Μάννα, ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν ἐλαίῳ [To brōma autou meli agrion, hou hē geusis ēn tou Manna, hōs enkris en elaiō]· His food was wild honey, with the taste of Manna, like a cake fried in oil. On this passage Epiphanius asserts that they set themselves this aim, to change the word of truth into a lie, and ἀντὶ ἀκρίδων ποιήσωσιν ἐγκρίδας ἐν μέλιτι [anti akridōn poiēsōsin enkridas en meliti], to make out of locusts cakes fried in honey. The occasion for this fabrication was taken from the fact that ἀκρίδες [akrides] and ἐγκρίδες [enkrides] are very similar words. And just as in the Gospel ἀκρίδες καὶ μέλι [akrides kai meli] are joined, so it is said of the Manna in Exod. XVI, 31.: And its taste was ὡς ἐγκρὶς ἐν μέλιτι [hōs enkris en meliti], like a cake fried in honey (or with honey). If John's food in the desert had tasted like that, it would not have been much proof of an austere life. Others think otherwise, namely that ἀκρίδες [akrides] in this passage are ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya], or τῶν φυτῶν ἀκρέμονας [tōn phytōn akremonas], the tips of trees and plants, on which John lived in that desert. Thus Isidore of Pelusium, in the fifth Letter of book 1, wants the monk, taught by John, to be content with ἀκρέμοσι βοτανῶν καὶ φυλλῶν πρὸς ὀλίγην τροφήν [akremosi botanōn kai phyllōn pros oligēn trophēn], the tips of plants and leaves for slender nourishment. And in Letter 132 he clings so tenaciously to this interpretation that he brings a charge against those who understand locusts by the name ἀκρίδες [akrides], in these words: Αἱ ἀκρίδες, αἷς Ἰωάννης ἐτρέφετο, οὐ ζῶά εἰσιν, ὥς τινες οἴονται ἀμαθῶς, κανθάροις ἀπεοικότα· μὴ γένοιτο. ἀλλ᾽ ἀκρέμονες βοτανῶν, ἢ φυτῶν [Hai akrides, hais Iōannēs etrepheto, ou zōa eisin, hōs tines oiontai amathōs, kantharois apeoikota; mē genoito. all᾽ akremones botanōn, ē phytōn]. Those acrides on which John fed are not animals resembling beetles, as some ignorantly suppose; far from it: but the tips of plants or trees. So also Paulinus, in his poem on John the Baptist:
Wild honey furnished easy sustenance, and fruits, and herbs sprung from untilled rocks.
